# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Need a movie for a Halloween weekend that's fun, not too scary. What should I watch?

**Score:** 34
**Body:** I want something spooky but not stay-up-all-night terrifying. I like dark comedy, a good twist and a strong lead character. I've already seen Hocus Pocus, Scream and Beetlejuice. What would you pick? Bonus points if it's a hidden gem.

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Shaun of the Dead 
2. Either of the Addams Family movies. The second one especially. Neither are spooky, but definitely dark comedy. 
3. Young Frankenstein (mel brooks movie)
4. Tremors
5. Army of Darkness, Coraline 
6. If you want an absolute classic Halloween movie, check out Arsenic and Old Lace. It’s set on Halloween and is an absolutely hysterical dark comedy. No horror elements.

If you want something more modern, check out Tucker and Dale vs. Evil. It’s a spoof of slasher movies with a little bit more gore.
7. The Burbs. 😁
8. The Monster Squad
9. The Frighteners (1996)

Fright Night (1985)
10. Dale and Tucker vs Evil

## 2. Benevolent "monsters" that are traditionally characterized as being evil?

**Score:** 36
**Body:** Basically I'm looking for examples where a "monster" character is the opposite of what they have usually have been portrayed, as in evil.  Films or tv shows where the "monsters" are friendly, have goodwill, and a genuine desire to help people even against other true monsters.  Obviously films like Blade, Hellboy, Teen Wolf or shows like The Munsters, True Blood and iZombie.

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Where The Wild Things Are! RIP Catherine O'Hara and James Gandolfini. The monsters are neither pure good nor pure bad. It's a great study of flawed characters bumping into each other, plus an awesome soundtrack from Karen O of the Yeah Yeah Yeahs. 
2. One of my all-time favorite X-Files episodes was the one about the freakshow monster that had a heart of gold and was an ultimate fan of the legendary *CHER!*
3. Edward Scissorhands. He's built like a horror movie creature, lives in the castle on the hill, and he's the gentlest person in the whole film. Burton flips it so the scary ones are the nice suburban neighbours. Still gets me every time.

And How to Train Your Dragon - if animation counts. Dragons are the classic beast you're supposed to slay, and the movie makes you care about one more than about most of the humans.
4. Come on guys,  Harry and the Hendersons is right there! 
5. Hellboy is kind of the ultimate version of this. He's literally a demon summoned to end the world and he grows up loving pancakes and fighting for the good guys. Del Toro's first one is my favorite.
6. Warm Bodies (2013) could fit, especially since you mentioned iZombie. R is a zombie who protects a human survivor, and the film leans into romance and comedy rather than straight horror. Are lighter takes on the idea welcome too?
7. "Pete's Dragon"   (the original movie from 1977) 
8. Frankenstein's monster in "The Monster Squad" (1987) is a perfect example of this.
9. Del Toro's Frankenstein has a very sympathetic monster, IMO.
10. The big friendly giant 

## 3. Semi-grounded movies that start simple and spiral out of control

**Score:** 23
**Body:** Like how Ferris Bueller's Day Off starts with him pretending to be sick to skip school, but by the end he's leading parades and stuff. I'm looking for stories where the plot is mostly advanced by ridiculous happenstance. I know I said grounded but I will actually also accept fantasy and sci-fi if it's still primarily driven by that sort of "series of accidents blowing up something simple" plot structure and not a "we have to kill the evil wizard" type of story (I like those too, but they're not what I'm looking for today).

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. *Sorry to Bother You* starts out as a fairly-straightforward black comedy/satire about racism in the workplace, and ends as... something else.
2. Dude, Where's My Car?  Starts out with two guys that wake up, wondering what happened to their car, and escalates from there.
  - And then?
3. Harold and Kumar go to White Castle!
4. The Big Lebowski, a man wants a new rug after a couple of thugs soil his because he shares a name with the guy they’re looking for. Next thing The Dude knows he’s delivering ransom money, hanging out with rich weirdos, and being chased by nihilists. 
5. Big Trouble in Little China

From Dusk Till Dawn

The Goonies
6. I haven’t actually seen the movie, but someone once called “After Hours” a movie in the “one damned thing after another” genre, which is such an apt description for a certain kind of movie.

Those are usually more action / thriller / chaos inspired plots though. For example—“Apocalypto.” It’s very graphically violent but also a real heart-pounder. 

Oh, and “Uncut Gems” is fantastic. Also pretty heart-racing and violent though. 

For more of a slapstick take on that kind of movie, I personally love “The Man Who Knew Too Little,” even though it had bad reviews on release. It’s much closer in tone to a Ferris Bueller movie.

“Sisters” is kind of fun for watching everything spiral.

I think that “Mr. Blandings Builds His Dream House” and its loose remake “The Money Pit” might match what you’re looking for.

I don’t fully know if I’m capturing what you’re thinking of.
7. More thriller/drama, but I always recommend The Invitation (2015) for this type of prompt. Without spoiling too much, it's like 2/3rds uncomfortable dinner party, and then goes totally off the rails.
8. Mother! Not necessarily grounded but very much spirals out of control. 
9. Very Bad Things, 1998

A Simple Plan, 1998

## 5. doom scrolling fried my brain, what movies can genuinely pull you in and make you forget your phone exists?

**Score:** 19
**Body:** I've genuinely tapped out on 10/10 acclaimed movies in record time just cuz nothing got going, i trust this sub's recommendations so ill give it a good 10-20 mins watch time before deciding, all i want is a movie thats cool in a unique way, or just extremely fun, no specific genre, in fact im not as high on movies that lean hard into only one sub-genre or niches, unless that niche is rly unique or cool. im into everything, but currently in the mood of something a lil more dark, thriller/horror/mystery, dont want something that makes your think too too hard but im down for creative/complex plots/writing, also i dont like snark in main characters, big deal breaker especially if they have no redeeming qualities. 

tldr: just the title, everything else is out the window if its interesting 

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Green Room (2015). 
2. Watched 2001 with my friend who had his attention span fried and he loved it. Simply put your phone in another room
  - Yeah dude there are many,  many great movies.  Phone in another room is the way
  - 2001 is absolutely fantastic and a masterpiece, but... it also has a lot of slow and quiet scenes. Someone with a self-professed fried attention span would absolutely start checking their phone at several points.

They might have to work up to this one.
3. I find the best movies for keeping you engaged are ones with some stakes and a destination.  
I know we are going somewhere and when we get there the movie will end.

Best example of this for me is Mad Max Fury Road.

I also like Sorcerer

Then there's short sharp movies with a lot of visual appeal. Like The Mask for example

Nobody and Normal for a bit of a Bob Odenkirk unlikely action hero double feature with a nice straightforward simple plot and a tidy run time.

For longer movies, I really recommend promising yourself a 15 intermission at the halfway point (look out for the end of an act at the midway they're easy to see when you're looking for them
4. Snowpiercer (2013)
5. Koyaanisqatsi.
6. Upgrade , Train to Busan , Escape Room
7. I know you said that you were in the mood for something dark but I’m going to recommend a Pixar movie: 

Hoppers (2026). 

I’m recommending it because the theme is related to what you are looking for. 

The main message is “it’s good to sit quietly in nature sometimes.” 
8. Blue is the warmest color, oldboy, tales of terror from tokyo trilogy, land of the dead, diary of the dead, claypot curry killers

## 4. On Digger and it’s budget

**Score:** 57
**Body:** I have been thinking about this a lot the last several weeks and have been finally inspired to write something after seeing the post asking how people would market Digger if it were up to them.

I have seen so much discourse about this film focusing on its budget, and I am more and more frustrated by it. If Digger had a different budget it would be a different movie. And whether that alternate movie would be good or bad is moot for discussion. It’s schrodingers’s movie and it doesn’t matter.

When I watched Digger, I could clearly see what that budget went to and it was one aspect of the movie that made it spectacular for me. Digger’s budget went to thousands of professionals who make their living in the entertainment industry. The meticulously detail and beauty in the practical sets was astounding for example. How many people and hours and how much skill did that take? That is what I want to see more of. Movies thrive when the industry thrives for all those involved making movies. Not only execs trying to sell studios to the highest bidding media conglomerate.

I am very sorry that Digger won’t make its budget back, but the money spent making the movie was not wasted in my opinion. It was used to employ thousands of people working in an increasingly difficult industry to make a living in. If you have heard Tom Cruise talk then you know about his passion for making movies and that he values every persons role making movies. He has commented before about how he feels a responsibility, when he is the top billing on a movie, for every persons livelihood working on that production. In front of and behind the camera.

I am so thrilled that movies like Obsession and Backrooms have been so wildly successful, but the lesson shouldn’t be that Studios stop funding large scale productions. Particularly original non-franchise productions. The lesson instead should hopefully be to encourage studios to promote and fund those filmmakers to have more resources for their creative vision going forward in their careers. Movies like Obsession employed a fraction of the people a movie like Digger does. Do we really want to promote opinions that would encourage Studios to only focus on movies that provide employment for fewer people? Do those larger budgets always equal great films that will stand the test of time? No. But they are still valuable to an industry that is the profession of millions of people from a a wide range of vocations. From gaffers, carpenters, caterers, vfx, electricians all the up to actors and directors.

I am so disheartened on subs like this one to see so many focused on analyzing or judging Digger from only the perspective of executive looking at their balance book. My hope is that viewers would consider a wider lens. To watch movies and appreciate all those people who make a movie behind the scenes. 90% of those working a movie won’t get paid based on how well the movie fares at the box office, but have fortunately already been paid for their labor and/or kept insurance while being able to do a job in the creative industry.

I love movies! So I personally will go see and support as many movies I can in theaters. From tiny independent movies to huge comic book franchises. As an avid movie goer, I am only concerned about the budget insofar as it encourages studios to fund more large scale original productions.

I know Digger isn’t a film that appeals to a larger audience. I wish it was. But if you are passionate enough to want to engage conversations about what did or did not go wrong the marketing a film, then I hope you are can also be passionate about the million other facets that go into making movies.

As for Digger being panned. Movie critics rely on movies being made and I think too many critics succeed at encouraging people not to see a movie instead encouraging critical discussions about movies. I always admired Roger Ebert’s talent for movie reviews. It seemed to me he always tried to find, in any movie, something that would appeal to at least some faction of movie goers. I think Ebert in that way showed a lot of respect for not only cinephiles, but also casual movie goers who had more specific tastes in movies.

And Finally I just have to say, I loved Digger. Thematically it has no shortage of ideas to inspire opinions and spark conversation. Aesthetically there were no shortage of choices to dissect for meaning or significance. I saw it again yesterday and found so many fascinating subtleties that I had missed on my first viewing!

All that to say, I wish I saw more discussions with opinions (positive or negative) about Digger focusing on those things and less discussion focusing on deriding the marketing and budget of Digger.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Our world is so commoditized that it makes anything not measurable as a success via profit margins deemed of little value. In doing so it strips so much out of our lives that enriches our existence. I will be so bold as to say Digger isn’t just an incredible work of art, but that it needs to exist (in contrast to the endless list of movies that serve no purpose but to fill airtime).

What’s strange to me is that most folks who are well versed in analyzing theatrical profitability in a studied and unbiased manner like Dan Murrell are still inexplicably penciling in 100 million marketing spend when in absolutely no universe was this movie marketed like a 150 million budget at all.

I work in NYC film marketing and while we didn’t work on the film directly I am very close with WB teams and there was nothing going on for this for the longest. Pulled it off festivals and no real marketing behind it, it’s about as “dumped” as a Tom Cruise release has been in 30 years. 

Most analysts are judging it based on what other films in this budget range typically spend on P&A but there is nothing in real life events and campaigns that in anyway shape or form back up claims of a 100 million marketing push. 

Personally I think Focus possibly spent more on Obsession marketing than WB did marketing Digger because they knew the commercial appeal of their product. And that movie cost Focus 1/10 of Digger’s neg to WB. That’s what sales/marketing does. They allocate resources based on where value is projected to be highest.

WB under Zaslav has had a habit of under marketing perceived duds even if they cost a lot. Happened to another leftist foreign Oscar winner director with Mickey 17. 

So the 100 million marketing number being cited everywhere is almost always caveated with “sources familiar with similar projects” and never actually confirmed budget for Digger’s P&A.

I’ll say IMAX and VistaVision releases ain’t cheap, but they’re also higher PLF formats which increase revenue so that is a justified spend if the bulk of the theatrical revenue is coming from those formats. 

But what I will say is unequivocally, NO MOVIE with a 100 million P&A budget only starts presales 2 weeks before release. Does not happen. Presales and marketing spend go hand in hand. 

The faster presales grow, the more fuel the studios put behind the campaigns. That’s why everything is always front loaded af. Big money pours in 14 days to release then if opening weekend pops, they keep it going, if not, shift resources to the next thing.

## 5. Wolf (1994) get ready to enjoy the hate

**Score:** 29
**Body:** PEAK James Spader. That’s the first thing. He’s at the absolute pinnacle of his powers. He’s squirming and repulsive, and you won’t be able to get enough of it.

It’s hard to think of a less likely place to start a supernatural horror, than the stuffy offices of some old-fashioned publishing house. Even by 90s standards, the place feels heavy, and stale.

Jack Nicholson plays the old boy senior editor Will Randall. Moderately successful, attractive wife, one of the big beasts of the office for whatever that’s worth. He’s not quite the alpha male, but he’s about to be challenged for what position he has, by a particularly sleazy young upstart; Stewart Swinton is the name of James Spader’s slippery skin suit.

The first time you’ll feel sick to your stomach is quite early in the film. Spader’s character does something reprehensible. Don’t worry, he’ll sicken you further later. He’s a slimeball of the highest order.

I won’t bore you with the supernatural aspects of the plot. Man gets bitten by wolf, changes happen, superpowers are explored. You could have guessed all that from the title. It’s about the least interesting part of the film, although it is very well done in places. Nicholson is more lupine than ever when he’s actually playing a wolf. No prosthetic teeth and hairy palms needed. He was made for this role. If there was ever a face made to snarl, it’s his.

Who could be more perfect to play Nicholson’s new love interest, but the ever feline Michelle Pfeiffer. She’s slightly too gorgeous for us to really believe she would be into the 20 years-her-senior book editor, but if we can suspend disbelief for werewolves in mahogany shelved publishing houses, we can manage it for this.

The twist comes when Nicholson realises he’s not the only one who can smell a fart at 200 yards. Suffice to say, human creeps don’t get nicer with added powers, and now there’s two big beasts stomping around the office.

Nicholson and his rival spend the remainder of the film having a pissing contest and trying to outmanoeuvre each other over some promotion or other. Spader does a bit too much thinking from somewhere inside his trousers, and the film turns into a sort of horrifying parody of Benny Hill at one point. You’ll hear Yakkety Sax in your head next time you watch it. Sorry.

Spader delivers one of the best lines of his career at one point. You’ll know it when you hear it. It’s not at all nice, but he absolutely nails it.

I won’t spoil it any further, give it a watch. Under a full moon ideally.

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. This was a vanity project, spearheaded by Nicholson -- he (Nicholson) had bankrolled author Jim Harrison (of *Legends of the Fall* fame) through his 1970s-1980s financial troubles, and, years later, Nicholson called in the favor, saying "I'm sort of interested in doing a film based on XYZ, Jim, please help."

Turns out Nicholson, fresh off his Batman/Eastwick/Endearment surge, called in **\*a lot\*** of favors -- director Mike Nichols (*The Graduate*), composer Ennio Morricone (countless), and of course Michelle Pfeiffer -- this is why the film has such an old-time-y noir feel.  Despite that, the screenplay doesn't have a lot of "there" there;  it's mostly atmospheric, and that's what I like about it, but the core narrative is simple, sparse, and not well developed.

Harrison wrote the first few drafts, inspired by an alleged real-life experience (per his own memoirs, he 'transformed' in an isolated snowbound cabin, howled, and leapt 10+ feet into the air, striking his head on the ceiling rafters), then quit, due to creative differences, leaving Wesley Strick to modify/polish the final product.  The full-blown villain + final conflict are mostly Strick's additions, to give it "a more traditional structure."  Supposedly it was more open-ended and philosophical in its original incarnation, leading to the disagreement(s).

I really do like this one, but I agree that it suffers certain flaws.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Why do so many reviews of You Can See Everything seem to give Elizabeth Holmes the benefit of the doubt?

**Score:** 271
**Body:** So here are some quotes from the sort of reviews I’m talking about

New York Times:

>Whether Holmes’s occasional blinks and tears in these chats are performative is open to question as are her grasp on language, truth, science and reality itself

Slashfilm:

> Don't go into this movie expecting to have answers to any questions you might have about either Holmes or Fielder, because you'll just end up coming out with more questions

Variety:

>What she tells Fielder, with an implacable conviction that suggests a belief in her own narrative that’s nothing short of monomaniacal, is that the device patented by Theranos, which she sold as “the iPod of health care,” could, in fact, host any blood test that existed. 

RogerEbert.com:

>Through Fielder’s interactions with Holmes, we learn that she genuinely thinks she’s never told a lie before, not even a white lie

ScreenDaily:

> Fielder, an enigmatic presence himself, goes into this project wanting to solve the mystery of Elizabeth Holmes. Three hours later, he is no closer to an answer

Josh Lewis on Letterboxd:

>Whether this is a document (monument) to the impossibility/unknowability of ever fully knowing what’s going on inside someone else’s mind, or an intimate portrait of a narcissistic grifter by a master manipulator whose finally met his match, I don't think the subjects, the filmmakers or we will ever fully know or agree on what exactly we've seen here.

Also, this isn’t a review, but AwardsWatch reported that

>In a Q&A after You Can See Everything’s premiere at The Telluride Film Festival, Fielder said he still doesn’t really know what to think of Elizabeth Holmes”

Over and over, I read reviews of the movie suggesting it’s about “ambiguity” or “how you can never really know what someone’s thinking” or “the limits of truth,” and that the Holmes case is some sort of impenetrable Rorschach test for us all to make up our own minds about.

I’m sorry, but I find this line of thinking to be absolutely insane! There is no mystery about who Elizabeth Holmes is! There are no questions left about her! “Guilty beyond a reasonable doubt” applies very firmly in her case!

I wonder, honestly, whether the people making these sorts of claims know anything about the Holmes story beyond the basics. Because if you take even an hour to research it, you’d know that, among other things:

I feel that the popularity of the genre was due to a particular social mileau of the period. Society was uncovering the scale of historic child abuse through Spotlight and other exposes. However, that social mileau has passed, and from about 2015 was a growing awareness that it was not something that could be treated primarily as historical, the sense of post-abuse justice was undercut, the uncovering was seen as compromised, the abuse is ongoing and still partially hidden. ## 5. Inglorious Basterds: The Cathartic Power of Cinematic Violence

**Score:** 7
**Body:** Note: Spoilers for the whole movie.

A couple of days ago I re-watched *Inglorious Basterds*, an old favourite of mine, with a group of people who hadn't watched it before. I had seen the film several times before, and from my very first watch had loved and enjoyed it without fully being able to articulate what made it work for me; beyond, that is, the obvious elements: Waltz's incredible performance, Pitt's comedic timing, scene after scene of whiteknuckled tension, the dialogue, the craft, et cetera.

The only element that didn't work for me, or rather, eluded my instinct and understanding altogether whenever I tried to consider it in totality with how the rest of the film made me feel, was the sudden and deliberate departure from history that ends the film, wherein Hitler and the entire German High Command is brutally killed off, and World War II is brought to a far swifter and significantly less casualty-causing end.

I never really quite knew what to make of that ending. I read several reviews and analyses that repeatedly belaboured the point that it was a fantastical historical retelling meant more to evoke a wishful "what-if" sentiment than, obviously, to depict any true historical events or people. I shrugged and accepted those explanations and moved on.

But in this most recent watch, the gestalt of it all hit me in the face with such strength and conspicuousness I couldn't believe I hadn't understood what Tarantino had been saying earlier. He is famously a fan of cinema and violence — or let me amend that to *cinematic* violence — to the point of his famous defence of it (["Because it's so much fun, Jan, get it!"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=St8iEpkcDJc)) being a meme at this point. Keeping that in mind, it was apparent to me on this rewatch of *Inglorious Basterds* that it is his most wholehearted, unremitting declaration of the catharsis that cinematic violence has the power to impart.

To state the obvious, it's a ridiculously violent film; in that the amount and sometimes also the nature of violence in it is ridiculous. It's also a film that is obsessed with the idea of cinema and its presence and influence in the given zeitgeist. Fassbender's character revolves around his intimate knowledge of German cinema, and practically the entire back half of the film is built upon the premiere of a film that is also, fittingly, celebrating the violence committed by a German soldier. Here is Tarantino making his point in the most overt, unsubtle manner: audiences love on-screen violence, even when it is repetitive to the point of being parodic... or maybe, *especially* then. I have read several critiques that insist Tarantino is making fun of us, the audience of the film, by having the audience-within-the-film (consisting of Nazis, I should remind you) being seen as enjoying a film that mostly is just shot after shot of, well, shot after shot. But that idea has never sat right with me; watching the sheer craft and intention with which the violence is orchestrated in the movie should make it clear to anyone watching, even those unfamiliar with Tarantino, that he loves his cinematic violence, and he uses it in almost the exact opposite way someone like Haneke would do it; to enrapture and create awe, not to pass judgment on his viewers. The audience enjoying the film-within-the-film is less a commentary on our own tastelessness and more a reaffirmation of Tarantino's own philosophy.

This philosophy is laid out in acute detail in the climax of the film, where a theatre full of Nazis is burned down, *while* the audience is also being shot at mercilessly like fish in a barrel by two Jewish guerrilla fighters. This entire sequence is pointedly over the top, including a shot that even in this film can be called gratuitous where an already dead Hitler's corpse is re-riddled with bullets; all of this while the film that the audience had been gleefully watching moments ago has been replaced by the "Giant Face" of a laughing Jewish woman who has fatally trapped them in her conflagration. Here is Tarantino laying down his cards in plain sight; here is him showing how much power a victim hijacking the cinema of her perpetrator can wield, both psychologically and literally; here is him also wrapping that particular scene up with violence so exaggerated and cartoonish it's hard to take it seriously, even when it takes the form of two men gunning down a convulsing crowd of theatregoers who are fruitlessly scrambling over each other for some form of safety. It is a sight that should, in most other contexts, horrify us; but both the foreknowledge of who are being killed here as well as the execution of the executions (see: Hitler's corpse) combine to tell us: this violence is not real. This violence is cinematic. The only thing real here is the catharsis you feel to see a grotesque evil unexpectedly defeated, even in a fictional manner.

What cinched this idea for me was a scene that happens pretty early on, where we first see the titular Basterds in action as they interrogate captured German officers. When the first prisoner refuses to collaborate, and is sentenced to die at the hands (bat) of the "Bear Jew", Pitt's character remarks, "Quite frankly, watchin' Donny beat Nazis to death is the closest we ever get to goin' to the movies." For his character, cinema and violence serve the same function: catharsis. If he we were a real person, this mindset would be troubling, to say the least. But he isn't. None of this is. That's why it's so much fun, Jan.

I hope I get my point across, I'm not really sure if I made much sense or if the feeling I had was articulated well through this post. Either way, interested to know how others feel about the ending, or the movie, or Tarantino's oeuvre in general.
